nodes.title: Classical and relative period annuli
nodes.statement: For S=Spa(F,O_F), identify the completion of B^b=A[1/pi,1/[varpi]] for the norms |sum_n[x_n]pi^n|_rho=sup_n |x_n| rho^n (0<rho<=1), and the separately defined norm |x|_0=q^(-v_pi(x)), with the parent interval ring after its radius conversion. The comparison preserves E-algebra operations, each interior norm, restrictions and Frobenius. For E=Q_p it is the upstream AdicSpaces Layer 6 ring B^I. If 1 belongs to I, E is given the discrete topology; if 1 does not belong to I, use its local-field topology. For rho=q^-r with 0<rho<1, the Banach E-norm is n_rho(x)=|x|_rho^(1/r), so n_rho(pi)=q^-1. At rho=0 use n_0=|.|_0. On a compact interval avoiding 1 take the maximum of these normalized endpoint norms; its topology is that of the original Gauss norms. The unnormalized Gauss norms are used for Newton calculus, not as E-homogeneous norms.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Use the imported ramified Witt construction and the absolute specialization of its annular charts.
Compare norms on the common dense localization and extend by separated completion.
For I containing 1 verify the induced norm on E is trivial; do not transport a Banach E-structure with the usual norm across this endpoint.

nodes.title: Ramified Gauss norm calculus
nodes.statement: On B^b each interior Gauss norm is multiplicative, nonarchimedean and independent of pi. It is given by the coefficient formula sup_n |x_n| rho^n; in particular |[a]|_rho=|a| and |pi|_rho=rho. These two values and multiplicativity alone are not a uniqueness assertion without the coefficient formula or a continuity hypothesis. For x in A and k>=0 put N_k(x)=max_(0<=n<=k)|x_n|. Then N_k(x+y)<=max(N_k(x),N_k(y)), N_k(xy)<=max_(i+j=k)N_i(x)N_j(y), N_k(pi x)=N_(k-1)(x) with N_(-1)=0, and N_k(phi x)=N_k(x)^q. These estimates pass to the completions. For rho=q^(-r), v_r(phi x)=q v_(r/q)(x).
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Derive coefficient bounds from homogeneity and integrality of the ramified Witt addition and multiplication polynomials.

For multiplicativity use the first minimizing indices n_0,m_0; the distinguished product coefficient is at index n_0+m_0, with pi exponent n_0+m_0. Its initial term cannot cancel. The printed product of the indices is corrected.
Compare the coefficient norms under uniformizer substitution using the Witt coefficient estimates and continuity; compute Frobenius on Teichmuller coefficients.
acceptance: Check [a]pi^n has norm |a|rho^n and Frobenius sends its norm to |a|^q rho^n, fixing the radius variance.

nodes.title: Radial limits and coefficient topology
nodes.statement: For x=sum[x_n]pi^n in B^b, the limits |x|_rho as rho approaches 0 from above and 1 from below recover respectively the pi-adic leading index and sup_n|x_n| in the precise rescalings v_r(x)/r -> v_pi(x) as r->infinity and v_r(x)->v_0(x):=inf_n v_F(x_n) as r->0. On A, every interior norm induces the imported weak topology, |.|_0 induces the pi-adic topology, and |.|_1 induces the [varpi]-adic topology; A is complete for all these norms. For mixed-characteristic E and epsilon near 1 but epsilon!=1, |[epsilon]-1|_1=1.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Bound the leading coefficient and the tail separately in the two limits; v_r is an infimum of affine functions.

Use the parent coefficient-topology theorem for interior radii. For endpoint 1 use the multiplicative [varpi]-adic filtration and coefficientwise convergence; the pi-adic endpoint is Witt completeness.
For the discontinuity test reduce the Witt subtraction identities and use Frobenius iteration; pointwise convergence of coefficients is insufficient for the supremum norm.
acceptance: The limits distinguish |.|_0 from the ordinary rho=0 substitution and distinguish weak convergence from endpoint-1 convergence.

nodes.title: Legendre transforms and Newton polygons
nodes.statement: Import proper lower-semicontinuous EReal-valued convex functions and Fenchel–Moreau duality from OptimalTransport Layer 5. In the real dual pair specialize its conjugate P* by L(P)(r)=-P*(-r)=inf_x(P(x)+rx), so P(x)=sup_r(L(P)(r)-rx). The source slope is the negative geometric derivative. For nonzero x in B^b define Newt(x) as the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex decreasing minorant of the coefficient data (n,v_F(x_n)), with value +infinity left of v_pi(x). Its epigraph is the closed convex hull of the upper vertical and right horizontal rays from those points. Its transform equals v_r(x) for r>=0, including the coefficient-infimum value at r=0; for r<0 it is -infinity. The separate norm at radius zero remains v_pi, not this r=0 value. Specialize infimal convolution to these polygons; finite-slope multiplicity is horizontal length. This node owns the polygon and sign bridge, not general convex duality.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Specialize the imported proper closed convex carrier to the real dual pair, retaining infinite endpoint values. Transport the generic conjugate identities through r |-> -r and output negation.

Adjoin upper vertical and right horizontal rays to the coefficient points before taking the closed convex hull. Supporting lines with nonpositive geometric slope and the coefficient formula give the Gauss transform for r>=0; the right rays force value -infinity for r<0.
Use imported biduality to recover the polygon from that transform; use closed infimal convolution when needed.
acceptance: The plus sign in the transform and the negative-geometric-slope convention give positive slopes for pi-[a] when 0<|a|<1.

sources.match: The plus sign in the transform and the negative-geometric-slope convention give positive slopes for pi-[a] when 0<|a|<1.

nodes.title: Newton products and Jensen formula
nodes.statement: For nonzero x,y in B^b, Newt(xy)=Newt(x) star Newt(y). Source slopes concatenate with horizontal multiplicity. For x=product_(i=1)^d(pi-[a_i]), all 0<|a_i|<1, the slopes are v_F(a_i), and v_r(x)=sum_i min(r,v_F(a_i)). In particular integrating the jumps of the one-sided derivatives recovers the change in v_r, the nonarchimedean Jensen identity.

proofSteps: Apply multiplicativity of Gauss norms and Legendre biduality.

nodes.title: Completed annuli and faithful restriction
nodes.statement: For nonempty I subset [0,1], B_I is the inverse limit of B_J over compact nonempty subintervals J of I. On compact [a,b] its topology is given by max(|.|_a,|.|_b); on a general interval it is complete and metrizable. A embeds as a closed subring. Every nonempty restriction B_I->B_J for J subset I is injective. When 0 belongs to I, B_I embeds in B_{0}=W_OE(F)[1/pi].
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Concavity of v_r gives the endpoint maximum principle and a countable cofinal family of compact subintervals.
Extend completion and inverse-limit maps on the common dense B^b.
To prove injectivity first stabilize the nonzero value and one-sided slopes at a radius inside J, then propagate concavity to rule out zero on another subinterval.

Before invoking normed E-space results, normalize every positive endpoint by the power 1/(-log_q rho); combine with the already normalized endpoint-zero norm. The resulting ultrametric norm is E-homogeneous and equivalent topologically to the endpoint Gauss family. Endpoint 1 is excluded from these functional-analytic imports.
acceptance: A restriction to a single radius remains injective; the result concerns these period rings, not an arbitrary function sheaf.

nodes.title: Newton data on completed annuli
nodes.statement: For 0!=f in B_I, define v_r(f)=-log_q|f|_(q^-r) at positive radii in I and define its left and right derivatives by stabilization from any B^b-approximating sequence. Newt_I(f) is the closed polygon determined by the restriction of this concave function, truncated to the slopes corresponding to I. At an interior slope r the multiplicity is partial_left v_r(f)-partial_right v_r(f), a nonnegative integer. At an included endpoint use its one-sided convention, including vertical rays; at radius 1 a zero slope may accumulate.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Show an approximation error with strictly larger valuation cannot change the first and last minimizing coefficient indices at a fixed radius.
Independence of approximants defines the derivatives, then Legendre duality defines the restricted polygon.
Specify endpoint half-lines explicitly before making assertions about multiplicity there.
acceptance: For an interior linear zero the derivative drops by one; on compact I avoiding 1 only finitely many nonzero slopes occur.

nodes.title: Uniform stabilization of approximating norms
nodes.statement: If f_n in B^b converges to nonzero f in B_I, then for every compact J subset I there is N such that |f_n|_rho=|f|_rho for every rho in J and n>=N. Consequently Newt_J(f) is realized by a single element of B^b, and completed Newton products still obey infimal convolution.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: First take J contained in (0,1]. Stabilize the nonzero endpoint valuations and the available one-sided derivatives; use the corresponding supporting lines to bound the valuation on the compact parameter interval.

Choose the approximation error above this uniform finite bound. The ultrametric inequality forces equality at every radius in J. This is the positive-radius argument of Proposition 1.6.16, with the corrected endpoint bound.

If 0 belongs to J, pi-adic convergence fixes an initial finite coefficient segment and v_pi(f_n)=v_pi(f). A bound at one positive radius controls the remaining tail near zero; its higher pi powers are strictly smaller than the fixed first nonzero term on a sufficiently short initial interval. Combine that interval with the positive-radius compact argument. A singleton {0} uses only pi-adic stabilization.
Apply the equality of all positive-radius norms to the restricted Newton polygon. At radius zero record the stabilized v_pi separately.
acceptance: The positive-radius proof supplies a uniform finite bound even for opposite endpoint derivatives. An included radius zero is treated separately by pi-adic coefficient stabilization and a positive-radius tail bound, rather than by applying Proposition 1.6.16 outside its hypotheses.

nodes.title: Coefficient extensions and radius rescaling
nodes.statement: Let Eprime/E be finite with ramification index e and residue degree f, and suppose F contains its residue field. Put Eprime_0=W_OE(F_(q^f))[1/pi]. Then B_(E,I) completed-tensor_(Eprime_0) Eprime is canonically B_(Eprime,I^(1/e)), with pi prime on the right and phi prime=phi^f. For compact I the ordinary tensor already suffices. Interior norm formulas use the chosen normalization qprime=q^f; at rho=0 the transported norm is the appropriate [Eprime:E]-power, not literal equality. The unramified case keeps the underlying ring and changes Frobenius to phi^f.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Apply the parent perfect-coefficient Witt tensor comparison to A and its localization.
Use a basis 1,pi prime,...,pi prime^(e-1) to compare completed norms and convert each radius.
Check finite-dimensional completeness for compact I and the iterated Frobenius on the unramified coefficient field.

nodes.title: Expansions at radius zero
nodes.statement: If 0 belongs to I and 1 does not, every f in B_I has a unique expansion sum_(n>=n0)[x_n]pi^n with x_n in F and |x_n|rho^n->0 as n->infinity for every positive rho in I. Under the common injection into B, B_[0,1]=B^b and its power-bounded subring is A. In mixed characteristic no assertion of existence, uniqueness or additivity of arbitrary two-sided Teichmuller expansions is made for B or B-plus.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Embed into the pi-adic complete field B_{0}, whose Teichmuller expansion is unique and bounded below in index.
Use interior coefficient bounds to characterize the image, then impose endpoint-1 boundedness.
Contrast with the two-sided series class: the nonlinear Witt carry limits need not converge under mere interior convergence.
acceptance: The uniqueness theorem is confined to intervals including 0; its extension to all B is not an available theorem.

nodes.title: Extension across either boundary
nodes.statement: Let I be an interval of positive radii. If 0 is in its closure, f extends uniquely to B_(I union {0}) exactly when Newt_I(f) is bounded to the left in its horizontal coordinate, equivalently pi^N f is bounded near 0 for some N. If 1 is in its closure, f extends uniquely to B_(I union {1}) exactly when its Newton polygon is bounded below, equivalently lim_(rho->1)|f|_rho is finite. The latter limit always exists in [0,infinity]. Both conditions give B_[0,1]=B^b. They do not imply extension across a missing boundary separated from the closure of I.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Split dense approximants into their positive and negative index parts for radius 0, and into bounded/unbounded coefficient valuations for radius 1.
Use stabilized norms and slope monotonicity to make the excluded part tend to zero on every compact interval.
Sum the differences in the boundary-completed ring; invoke faithful restriction for uniqueness.
acceptance: Extension requires the boundary to be a limit point; a relatively compact annulus alone carries no such extension assertion.

sources.match: Extension requires the boundary to be a limit point; a relatively compact annulus alone carries no such extension assertion.

nodes.title: Newton criterion for units
nodes.statement: For 1 not in I, a nonzero f in B_I is a unit exactly when Newt_I(f) has no finite slope corresponding to a radius of I. For 1 in I it must have only possible slope 0 at that boundary and a finite right derivative there. Units extend across each boundary in the closure of I. In particular B^times=(B^b)^times and R^times=(E-dagger)^times, where R=colim_(rho->0) B_(0,rho] and E-dagger=colim B_[0,rho].
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: On a slope-free compact interval factor out the uniquely dominant monomial and invert 1+h by a convergent geometric series.
Glue these inverses by faithful restriction and impose finite index at endpoint 1.
Apply both boundary-extension criteria to f and its inverse, then pass to the filtered union at 0.
acceptance: A nonzero constant is a unit, a linear factor fails precisely on an interval containing its zero radius, and endpoint 1 requires its extra finite-index condition.

nodes.title: Overconvergent field and Robba germs
nodes.statement: Identify the imported overconvergent bounded ring and Robba ring with E-dagger and R in the preceding colimits, for general perfect F and either characteristic of E. E-dagger is a Henselian discretely valued field for v_pi, with residue field F and completion W_OE(F)[1/pi]. For finite L/F the extension E-dagger_L/E-dagger_F has degree [L:F]. For F the completed perfection of k((t)), compare with the completed perfected classical bounded and Robba rings using the inverted-radius convention.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Compute the residue field and discrete valuation from the boundary-0 expansion.
Solve a simple-root polynomial equation by Newton iteration on a sufficiently short annulus, shrinking that annulus once for the finitely many coefficient bounds.
Lift a residue-field basis for finite L/F and compare completions to compute the degree. The comparison with RD.0 does not import its discretely-valued-coefficient PID theorem for arbitrary F.

If min I=rho>0, the underlying algebras B_I^plus, B_rho^plus, B_[rho,1)^plus and B_[rho,1]^plus agree, with the last topology generally strictly stronger.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.

Define the intersection with its induced Frechet topology and distinguish algebraic identification from topological equivalence.

nodes.title: Newton characterization of positivity
nodes.statement: A nonzero f belongs to B_rho^plus exactly when its extended Newton polygon over [rho,1] lies in the nonnegative vertical half-plane, equivalently it extends to radius 1 with |f|_1<=1. B^plus is the corresponding intersection over rho and is the largest subring of B_rho^plus on which phi is bijective: B^plus=intersection_(n>=0) phi^n(B_rho^plus). This agrees with the classical B_rig^plus notation after the specified comparison.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Use the closure description to bound coefficients vertically, then apply boundary extension.
Frobenius carries rho to rho^q and preserves nonnegative coefficient valuations.
Intersect the expanding domains under inverse Frobenius and use the same coefficient criterion.
acceptance: Positivity is the coefficient bound |.|_1<=1 after extension, not the condition v_pi(f)>=0.

nodes.title: Monomial completed-perfection model
nodes.statement: Let k/F_q be perfect, F the completion of k((t^(1/p^infinity))), |t|=q^-1, T=[t]. Identify A with sums sum_(alpha>=0 in Z[1/p]) a_alpha T^alpha, a_alpha in W_OE(k), such that for every n and every real bound M only finitely many alpha<M have a_alpha nonzero modulo pi^n. This is the weak (pi,T)-adic completion of the perfected polynomial model, with coefficients already pi-adically complete. For interior rho=q^-r, |sum a_alpha T^alpha|_rho=sup_alpha q^(-r v_pi(a_alpha)-alpha). In B_I allow alpha in Z[1/p] and rational coefficients W_OE(k)[1/pi], requiring these terms to tend to zero off finite sets at each interior radius, with the extra boundary bounds.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Use the coefficientwise description of O_F and then lift successively modulo pi^n.
Apply the coefficient filtration N_k to identify the norm of each monomial and the supremum formula.
Complete the common Laurent algebra for all radii in I; impose bounded coefficient valuations at 0 and support bounded below at 1.
acceptance: The weak completion allows arbitrarily high t-order tails; pi-adic completion of the bare polynomial ring is insufficient.

sources.match: The weak completion allows arbitrarily high t-order tails; pi-adic completion of the bare polynomial ring is insufficient.

nodes.title: Perfected annulus towers and norm powers
nodes.statement: For the monomial model set K0=W_OE(k)[1/pi] with |pi|=q^-1, and send X to T. With rho=q^-r and checkrho=q^(-1/r), |i(f)|_rho=||f||_checkrho^r, where ||.|| is the ordinary K0-Gauss norm. The completed direct limit of the annulus algebras under X->X^q, with transformed intervals and norms, is B_I. The dense initial Laurent algebra must invert both pi and X. In characteristic zero the annulus tower is finite etale; in equal characteristic p the q-power tower is radicial.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Evaluate both sides on pi and X, then on arbitrary convergent Laurent series.
Use the monomial description to prove density and completion.
Differentiate X^q to separate the characteristic-zero etale assertion from its characteristic-p failure.
acceptance: The r-th power is essential: the printed literal isometry fails already on pi. In characteristic p the tower is not etale.

sources.match: The r-th power is essential: the printed literal isometry fails already on pi. In characteristic p the tower is not etale.

nodes.title: Cyclotomic coordinates on period annuli
nodes.statement: For E=Q_p (q=p), use the Frobenius lift Q(X)=(1+X)^q-1 and the embedding X->[1+t]-1. For an ordinary annulus radius s>q^(-q/(q-1)), write s=q^(-1/r), so the period radius is rho=q^-r<q^(-(q-1)/q). In this range ||f||_s=|i(f)|_rho^(1/r). The completed perfected cyclotomic tower identifies with B_I for I contained in that strict period-radius range. For a ramified coefficient field the detailed Newton slopes must use v_pi(p) and the p-Frobenius iteration; no unramified slope formula is asserted for arbitrary E.
hypotheses: E=Q_p for the displayed numerical radius and cyclotomic-coordinate theorem. For general mixed-characteristic E the target is the corresponding comparison after deriving a threshold from the actual ramified carry polygon, recorded as G-COORDINATE.
proofSteps: Compare [1+t]-1 with [t] on the stated short period annulus, using the Newton polygon of the cyclotomic element.
Transport the monomial comparison with its norm power and inverted radius.
Use the correct strict transformed threshold; separate the coefficient-ramification dependence of the auxiliary Newton calculation.
acceptance: For E=Q_p, q=p, the ordinary radius threshold and its transformed period radius agree through s=q^(-1/r); the printed untransformed bound is not reused.

sources.match: For E=Q_p, q=p, the ordinary radius threshold and its transformed period radius agree through s=q^(-1/r); the printed untransformed bound is not reused.

nodes.title: Equal-characteristic exchange of variables
nodes.statement: For E=F_q((pi)), B_I is the ordinary Laurent annulus algebra with coefficient field F and variable pi, with precisely the source boundary conditions. More generally for perfect k and E0=k((u)), F0=k((v)), exchange the two indices of a doubly convergent Laurent expansion to identify O(D_E0^*) and O(D_F0^*) as Frechet k-algebras. The Gauss parameters r and 1/r are exchanged and their numerical norms differ by the corresponding r-th power. The associated adic spaces are the common locus Spa(k[[u,v]],k[[u,v]]) minus V(uv), viewed over either valued field.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Apply the imported Laurent-annulus construction for the first assertion.
On compact radial intervals bound the double family of coefficients to justify transposing convergent sums.
Compute u^a v^b on both sides to determine the power of the norm and identify the common formal adic chart.
acceptance: The symmetry is k-linear and topological; it is not a norm-preserving map with fixed numerical normalization on both coefficient fields.

sources.locator: Example 1.6.5, p. 70; Proposition 1.7.4 and Remark 1.7.5, pp. 83–84
sources.match: The symmetry is k-linear and topological; it is not a norm-preserving map with fixed numerical normalization on both coefficient fields.

nodes.title: Hahn-series period rings
nodes.statement: Let Gamma be a nonzero subgroup of R with p Gamma=Gamma and F=k((t^Gamma)) the Hahn field of well-ordered support. In A write sum_(alpha in Gamma_nonnegative) a_alpha T^alpha with a_alpha in W_OE(k), whose nonzero support modulo pi^n is well ordered for every n. For interior I, B_I uses coefficients in W_OE(k)[1/pi] and, for every rho in I and positive c, the exponents on which |a_alpha|_rho q^-alpha>=c form a well-ordered set. The topology and Gauss norms are given by these coefficient bounds. Endpoint radii require the additional boundedness conditions, not merely interior convergence.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Use the Hahn support condition to lift O_F through each truncated Witt ring.
Pass to the filtered union after inverting pi and T and complete at interior norms.
Verify the support condition is stable under the ramified Witt operations using finite truncations; compute the norm by N_k.
acceptance: The coefficient pi^-1 must be present in B_I, contradicting the printed formula with only integral W_OE(k)-coefficients.

sources.match: The coefficient pi^-1 must be present in B_I, contradicting the printed formula with only integral W_OE(k)-coefficients.

nodes.title: Ramified Witt covectors and bivectors
nodes.statement: For a discrete F_q-algebra R, define the unipotent covectors CWu(R)=colim_V W_OE,n(R); full covectors allow a negative tail generating a nilpotent ideal. Put BW(R)=lim_V CW(R), and BW(O_F)=lim_(0!=a ideal O_F) BW(O_F/a). It is an O_E-module whose elements have unique formal coefficients sum_(n in Z)[a_n]pi^n with a_n in O_F and liminf_(n->-infinity) q^n v_F(a_n)>0. Summation embeds this module in B^plus. Addition is the limit of the ramified Witt addition polynomials with the required q-power twists.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Construct CW and BW as limits of the imported truncated ramified Witt functor, using Verschiebung transition maps.
Translate eventual nilpotence modulo every nonzero ideal into exponential growth of negative-tail valuations.
The stronger growth makes the Witt carry limits converge and yields an injective summation map; this does not extend to every two-sided convergent Teichmuller series.
acceptance: The negative-tail growth condition is stronger than convergence for each linear Gauss weight.

sources.locator: §1.10.2, Definition 1.10.11 and the coefficient/addition formulas, pp. 92–93
sources.match: The negative-tail growth condition is stronger than convergence for each linear Gauss weight.

nodes.title: Radius-dependent crystalline period rings
nodes.statement: Assume E=Q_p and rho in |F^times|, 0<rho<1. Let a_rho={x in O_F:|x|<=rho} and b_rho=ker(W(O_F)->O_F/a_rho). Define A_cris,rho as the p-adic completion of the divided power envelope of b_rho compatible with the canonical divided powers on (p); put B_cris,rho^plus=A_cris,rho[1/p]. It is the pro-final p-adic PD thickening computing degree-zero crystalline sections, not a terminal object among individual nilpotent thickenings.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Import the generic PD envelope and its completed universal property.
Choose a with |a|=rho; express the envelope inside W(O_F)[1/p] by the divided powers [a]^n/n!.
Compare the p-power truncations with the crystalline site and pass to the pro-object.
acceptance: The construction is restricted to E=Q_p and retains the pro-object qualification in its site interpretation.

sources.match: The construction is restricted to E=Q_p and retains the pro-object qualification in its site interpretation.

nodes.title: Crystalline and holomorphic invariant periods
nodes.statement: For E=Q_p, B_(rho^p)^plus is contained in B_cris,rho^plus, which is contained in B_rho^plus. Consequently B^plus=intersection_(n>=0) phi^n(B_cris,rho^plus). For a finite-dimensional isocrystal D over W(k)[1/p], k a perfect subfield of O_F (so the induced valuation on k is trivial), and a nonzero t in B_cris,rho^plus with phi(t)=pt, the phi-fixed vectors in D tensor B^plus[1/t] and D tensor B_cris,rho^plus[1/t] coincide.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Compare divided-power factorial denominators with the p-adic unit-ball presentation of each positive-radius ring.
Iterate Frobenius and use the characterization of its maximal bijective subring.
Use the finite-dimensional Frobenius matrix on D to move a fixed vector through all iterated radii after multiplying by one common power of t.

For the arbitrary perfect subfield k, use the pinned WittVector.Isocrystal structure on the fraction field of W(k), with a separate finite-dimensionality hypothesis. Its usual W(k)[1/p] comparison follows from the Witt DVR structure. VB0 fixes the different coefficient field breve E and cannot supply this arbitrary-k carrier.
acceptance: The equality is of invariant periods after the indicated localization, not equality of B^plus and B_cris,rho^plus.

sources.match: The equality is of invariant periods after the indicated localization, not equality of B^plus and B_cris,rho^plus.

nodes.title: The local boundary valuation quotient
nodes.statement: In B^{b,plus}=A[1/pi], put p_boundary={x:v_0(x)>0}, with v_0(x)=inf_n v_F(x_n), and m_boundary={sum[x_n]pi^n: every v_F(x_n)>0}. Define barB=B^{b,plus}/p_boundary. It is a local domain with maximal ideal m_boundary/p_boundary and residue field W_OE(k_F)[1/pi]. Frobenius is bijective on it and the quotient map extends to B^plus.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: The coefficient-infimum norm is multiplicative, hence p_boundary is prime.
If one coefficient is a unit, invert its reduction and solve successively modulo the uniformly positive ideal.

For 0<rho<1 restrict B^plus to B_[rho,1]^plus, then to B_1^plus. The latter completed positive ring has the coefficient-infimum valuation; quotienting its ideal v_0>0 gives the same algebraic barB as A[1/pi]. Compose these maps to extend the quotient map. This does not assign an inherited Banach topology to quotient eigenspaces.
acceptance: Uniform positivity defining p_boundary differs from positivity of every coefficient defining m_boundary.

sources.match: Uniform positivity defining p_boundary differs from positivity of every coefficient defining m_boundary.

nodes.title: Q-compatible inverse limits
nodes.statement: For a pi-adically complete O_E-algebra R and Q in O_E[X] with Q(0)=0 and Q congruent to X^q modulo pi, let R^{flat,Q} be the set of sequences (x_n) with Q(x_(n+1))=x_n. Transport its perfect F_q-algebra structure from lim_(Frob_q) R/pi via reduction. Its zeroth projection is multiplicative for the monomial Q=X^q, but for a general Q it is not asserted to be an additive or multiplicative ring map. The construction is canonically independent of Q after passage to the common reduced inverse limit.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Lift a compatible residue sequence by successive Q-iteration; the congruence gain makes the lifts Cauchy.
Prove independence of lifts and uniqueness using pi-adic separatedness.
Transport addition, multiplication and inverse Frobenius from the perfection inverse limit, checking functoriality in R.
acceptance: The Q-compatible sequence set is given its ring structure through reduction, rather than coordinatewise addition.

sources.locator: Definition 2.1.1, Proposition 2.1.2, Lemma 2.1.3, Corollary 2.1.4 and Remark 2.1.5, pp. 98–100

nodes.title: Reduction invariance of the Q-limit
nodes.statement: If J is a closed ideal of R and R is complete for (J,pi), then reduction induces a bijection R^{flat,Q}->(R/J)^{flat,Q}. In particular the preceding comparison with the perfection of R/pi is valid. For a perfect F_q-algebra S, the Q-Teichmuller map identifies S with the Q-compatible inverse limit of W_OE(S).
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: For congruent lifts use Q(x)-Q(y) in pi(x-y)+(x-y)^q to increase the (J,pi)-adic precision under iteration.
Construct compatible coordinates by a diagonal limit and show all choices have the same limit.
Apply the ramified twisted Teichmuller uniqueness in the perfect Witt case.
acceptance: The completeness condition is (J,pi)-adic and the ideal is closed; an arbitrary quotient is not enough.

sources.match: The completeness condition is (J,pi)-adic and the ideal is closed; an arbitrary quotient is not enough.

nodes.title: Ramified Fontaine map for complete algebras
nodes.statement: For pi-adically complete R as above construct theta_Q:W_OE(R^{flat,Q})->R using the Q-twisted Witt ghost polynomials and the compatible-coordinate limits. It commutes with continuous algebra maps and with the Q-change identification. If Frobenius on R/pi is surjective, theta_Q is surjective. For E=Q_p and Q=X^p this map equals Mathlib WittVector.fontaineTheta on the existing PreTilt carrier, after the canonical inverse-limit identification. No new p-typical theta or Tilt carrier is introduced.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Define compatible finite theta_n using twisted ghost components; Lemma 2.1.6 gives divisibility bounds making the coordinate limit converge.
Check the ring identities at finite levels and pass to the limit.
For surjectivity lift a residue preimage and correct one pi-adic digit at a time; compare the p-typical case by the Teichmuller characterization.
acceptance: The general ramified map restricts to the actual pinned p-typical construction and has the stated surjectivity hypothesis.

sources.match: The general ramified map restricts to the actual pinned p-typical construction and has the stated surjectivity hypothesis.

nodes.title: Principal kernel criterion for theta
nodes.statement: Assume R is pi-torsion-free. If a=sum_n[a_n]_Q pi^n lies in ker theta_Q and the zeroth untilt coordinate of a_0 is pi times a unit of R, then ker theta_Q=(a). If pi has a compatible system of Q-roots represented by varpi in R^{flat,Q}, the kernel is generated by [varpi]_Q-pi. These are algebraic kernel assertions, with the induced pi-adic quotient topology.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Reduce modulo pi to divide an arbitrary kernel element by a_0 in the perfect inverse-limit algebra.
Subtract the multiple of a and iterate after dividing by pi, using torsion-freeness to preserve the kernel condition.
Sum the coefficients in the complete Witt ring; specialize to the chosen Q-root system.
acceptance: The kernel generator is conditional on torsion-freeness and the pi-times-unit hypothesis; the special [varpi]_Q-pi formula requires compatible roots.

sources.match: The kernel generator is conditional on torsion-freeness and the pi-times-unit hypothesis; the special [varpi]_Q-pi formula requires compatible roots.

nodes.title: Primitive equations of arbitrary degree
nodes.statement: For a=sum_(n>=0)[a_n]pi^n in A define PrimitiveDegree(a,d) by a_0!=0, a_d a unit of O_F, and a_i in m_F for every i<d. Equivalently a is not divisible by pi and the reduction to W_OE(k_F) has pi-order d. Primitive equations form a graded multiplicative monoid, degree zero is A^times, and irreducible primitive means positive degree with no factorization into two positive-degree primitive equations. Degree-one equations and their untilts are imported from RF2.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Use the reduction to the residue-field Witt DVR to read the first unit coefficient.
Multiply reductions to prove additivity of degree and compare constant coefficients to exclude pi-divisibility.
Relate the condition to the horizontal and positive segments of the Newton polygon.
acceptance: Primitivity includes a nonzero constant coefficient; pi itself is not primitive.

sources.match: Primitivity includes a nonzero constant coefficient; pi itself is not primitive.

nodes.title: Weierstrass division at a degree-one untilt
nodes.statement: Assume F algebraically closed and a primitive of degree 1. For D=A/(a), the imported untilt theorem identifies D with the valuation ring of an algebraically closed complete untilt C. Every element of D is theta([x]) for x in O_F, every element has an n-th root for n>=1, and theta([x])=theta([y]) implies v_F(x)=v_F(y). The ideal (a) has a generator [c]-pi. Every b in A has b=wa+[d], d in O_F; the remainder representative d is not unique. More generally b has a convergent a-adic expansion sum_(n>=0)[d_n]a^n.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Use the parent untilt equivalence and preservation of algebraic closedness under tilting, rather than the incomplete special p=2 root calculation in the classical proof.
Choose compatible q-power roots in C for a given element, using algebraic closedness and completeness to obtain a Teichmuller value.
Lift the value of pi to get the linear generator; divide by matching a Teichmuller residue and iterate.
acceptance: Division supplies an existing element and a Teichmuller remainder, with no false uniqueness claim for that remainder.

sources.locator: Lemma 2.2.3, Proposition 2.2.6, Corollaries 2.2.8–2.2.12, Lemmas 2.2.13–2.2.14 and Proposition 2.2.16, pp. 105–111
sources.match: Division supplies an existing element and a Teichmuller remainder, with no false uniqueness claim for that remainder.

nodes.title: Primitive points and marked untilts
nodes.statement: Let Y_cl be the set of irreducible primitive principal ideals of A. Its degree-one locus is canonically the parent classical-untilt point set. For a degree-one point y, the quotient A/p_y and its localization are O_(C_y) and C_y, and theta_y extends to B^b. Normalize v_y by v_y(theta_y([x]))=v_F(x); then v_y(pi)=v_F(a_0) for a degree-one generator. This normalization usually differs from the local-field normalization of E. Over algebraically closed F all degree-one residue fields are algebraically closed, and the cyclotomic polynomials split there. For the Q_p construction with F algebraically closed, spherical completeness of F implies spherical completeness of C_y.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Compare the parent kernel ideal and the classical principal ideal using the primitive-kernel criterion.
Localize and use the untilt valuation to identify the completed residue field.
Apply algebraic closedness for roots of unity; a separate generic rank-one solvability theorem is unnecessary along this proof route.

For spherical completeness, a chain of closed balls whose radii tend to zero is settled by completeness. Otherwise rescale into the valuation ring and a range below v_y(p); the sharp map modulo p identifies the needed truncated valuation balls with balls in F. A common point there lifts to a point in all the original balls. This uses the imported untilt quotient and valuation comparison, not a second construction of tilting.
acceptance: The valuation preserves the F-Teichmuller normalization and need not give v_y(pi)=1.

sources.locator: Definition 2.3.1, pp. 114–115; Proposition 2.2.15 and Corollary 2.2.22, pp. 109–114; Corollary 2.2.23, p. 114
sources.match: The valuation preserves the F-Teichmuller normalization and need not give v_y(pi)=1.

nodes.title: Valuative proximity of degree-one points
nodes.statement: For degree-one points y,z with p_z=(a_z), define delta(y,z)=v_y(theta_y(a_z)) in [0,infinity], independent of the primitive generator. It is symmetric, equals infinity exactly on the diagonal, and satisfies delta(y,w)>=min(delta(y,z),delta(z,w)). Thus d(y,z)=q^(-delta(y,z)), with q^-infinity=0, is an ultrametric. For a_r={b in A:v_0(b)>=r}, delta(y,z) is the largest r with p_y+a_r=p_z+a_r; this equality identifies the corresponding truncated untilt valuation rings.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.

nodes.statement: For a Lubin–Tate polynomial Q with Q congruent pi X modulo X^2 and Q congruent X^q modulo pi, and 0!=epsilon in m_F, set u_epsilon=Q([epsilon^(1/q)]_Q)/[epsilon^(1/q)]_Q=[epsilon]_Q/[epsilon^(1/q)]_Q and y_epsilon=(u_epsilon). It is primitive of degree one, with reduction epsilon^(1-1/q). The formal Lubin–Tate group on m_F gives an E-Banach space V with pi acting by q-Frobenius. For E=Q_p and Q=(1+X)^p-1, u_epsilon=sum_(i=0)^(p-1)[(1+epsilon)^(i/p)]. Normalize |pi|_E=q^-1 and use ||epsilon||_V=1/v_F(epsilon) for epsilon!=0, with ||0||_V=0. Then ||pi dot epsilon||_V=q^-1||epsilon||_V; the ordinary absolute value |epsilon|_F would not be a homogeneous E-vector norm.

nodes.title: Lubin–Tate parametrization and topology
nodes.statement: For F algebraically closed, epsilon |-> y_epsilon induces a bijection (V minus {0})/O_E^times -> Y_degree1. Give the source quotient the valuative proximity sup_(a in O_E^times) v_F(epsilon_1-a dot epsilon_2), using ordinary subtraction in F after the formal scalar action. It is at least q/(q-1) times delta(y_1,y_2), and the bijection is a homeomorphism. Modding by pi^Z yields P_E(V) homeomorphic to Y_degree1/phi^Z. The induced isomorphism C_y->C_(phi^k y) scales the F-normalized valuation by q^k, not by 1.

Equality of ideals is equality of the corresponding rank-one Tate submodules, hence precisely an O_E-unit orbit.
Compare valuations of the finite-level torsion polynomials, then pass to their inverse limit to prove the inequality and inverse continuity; compute Frobenius directly on [x].

nodes.title: Metric and Berkovich topologies
nodes.statement: Embed the degree-one classical points into the multiplicative seminorm spectrum of B^b by f |-> q^(-v_y(f)/v_y(pi)). Equip that spectrum with pointwise convergence and require restriction to E to be the fixed pi-adic norm. The induced topology on the degree-one locus equals its metric topology. Gauss points are normalized by v_r/r. The proof uses min(v_y(f),delta)=min(v_z(f),delta) for f in A and delta=delta(y,z), not the false lower bound v_y(f)-v_z(f)>=delta.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Continuity of evaluation on B^b follows from the norm bound at rho=|pi|_y.

First use equality below the common truncation precision only for f in A. Extend continuity to B^b by inverting pi and nonzero Teichmuller elements, whose evaluations never vanish, and divide by the continuous positive function y |-> v_y(pi). The truncated identity itself is not asserted on B^b.
For the reverse topology write a metric ball through the valuation of a primitive generator, adjusting for the continuous normalization denominator.

nodes.title: Primitive points under totally ramified coefficient change
nodes.statement: Let Eprime/E be finite separable and totally ramified and F algebraically closed. The determinant norm from A_Eprime to A_E sends a degree-one primitive equation to a degree-one primitive equation. Contraction gives Y_(Eprime),degree1->Y_E,degree1 with residue-field isomorphisms and fibres of cardinality [Eprime:E]. If the extension is Galois, each fibre is a Gal(Eprime/E)-torsor. The degree-one assertion concerns ramified Witt primitive degree, not multiplication of that degree by [Eprime:E].
hypotheses: Eprime/E finite totally ramified and separable; automatic in the mixed-characteristic source setting.
F algebraically closed.
proofSteps: Compute the determinant norm modulo pi using the finite free ramified Witt coefficient basis.
Use the untilt tensor decomposition over the algebraically closed residue untilt to identify the factors and contraction.
Count the embeddings of the separable local-field extension and identify the Galois action.

Separability is essential for the fibre cardinality and torsor statement; no such cardinality is asserted for a purely inseparable equal-characteristic coefficient extension.

nodes.title: Factorization of primitive equations
nodes.statement: If F is algebraically closed, every primitive a in A of degree d>=1 is a product of exactly d degree-one primitive elements. Equivalently a=u product_(i=1)^d([c_i]-pi), with u in A^times and 0<|c_i|<1. Thus irreducible primitive equations have degree one.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Let lambda be the least positive source slope. Choose a root of the coefficient polynomial in F of valuation lambda to obtain a first approximate untilt zero.

Expand a in powers of the current primitive generator and choose the root of largest valuation in the next finite coefficient polynomial. The evaluation precision rises by lambda while the proximity grows at least linearly in the iteration index.
The points stay on v_y(pi)=lambda; bounded-point completeness gives a zero. Divide by its degree-one equation and induct on d.

nodes.title: Evaluation and closed primitive ideals
nodes.statement: For degree-one y with ||y||=q^(-v_y(pi)) in I, evaluation theta_y extends continuously B_I->C_y, satisfies |theta_y(f)|<=|f|_(||y||), and has kernel m_y B_I. Multiplication by a primitive generator has closed image; division of an element in that image respects every compact annular norm. On B_I^plus use its corresponding primitive ideal. If lambda=v_y(pi) is not a slope of f in B^b, v_y(f)=v_lambda(f).
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Bound every Teichmuller summand by its Gauss value at ||y|| and complete.
Use the imported Cartier-divisor norm estimate to divide a Cauchy sequence of multiples and obtain a Cauchy sequence of quotients.
For the no-slope equality a unique dominant term survives evaluation, or apply the ordinary Laurent-series version in C_y.

nodes.title: A zero at every Newton slope
nodes.statement: Assume F algebraically closed. For nonzero f in B_I and every positive source slope lambda of Newt_I(f), there is y in Y_I with v_y(pi)=lambda and f(y)=0. One can divide off a degree-one primitive equation for y in B_I. For finitely many slopes listed with multiplicity one can divide off the corresponding product; the remaining polygon deletes exactly those segments.

proofSteps: For f in A truncate its Teichmuller expansion and use primitive factorization to choose zeros at the prescribed slope.
A uniform bound on the multiplicity at that slope forces a neighboring zero to approach each chosen zero; the proximity bound tends to infinity.
Pass to general B_I using compact norm stabilization and closed division, then iterate for finite multiplicities.

nodes.title: Geometric compact annuli and principal ideals
nodes.statement: Over algebraically closed F, compare the source compact interval ring with the imported geometric affinoid PID theorem whenever its endpoints define an annular affinoid. Extend the comparison to arbitrary compact I subset [0,1): I={0} and I={rho} with rho not in |F^times| give complete fields; every other I gives a PID with maximal spectrum Y_I. The integral subring {f in B_[0,rho]:v_pi(f)>=0}, 0<rho<1, is a PID with the extra maximal ideal (pi).
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Import the geometric affinoid PID theorem through the ring comparison, without adding a second affinoid-PID target.
For arbitrary compact I use the finite number of Newton slopes and linear-zero extraction to factor every nonzero element into a unit and finitely many point generators.
Use evaluation kernels to identify the primes and the factorization criterion for a PID; for a singleton with no allowed slope every nonzero element is invertible.

nodes.title: Weierstrass products near radius zero
nodes.statement: For a finite or countable family 0!=z_i in m_F, tending to zero if infinite, define W=product_i(1-[z_i]/pi), with empty product 1. The product converges in B^plus, uniformly for every compact positive-radius interval. For a nonzero f in B_I whose radii approach 0, list all zeros below a fixed rho_0 with multiplicity and choose their linear generators pi-[z_i]. Then f=Wg with g in B_(I union {0}) and no zeros below rho_0. If f in B_(0,1], then g in B^b; if f in B^plus, then g in A[1/pi].

proofSteps: On a compact J, the norm of [z_i]/pi tends uniformly to zero, so the nonarchimedean product converges.
Divide successively by the selected linear factors; the Newton norm formula bounds the quotient norms.
Show the quotient differences tend to zero on every compact J. The zero-free near-0 remainder extends by the boundary theorem.

nodes.statement: For I subset (0,1), define Div(Y_I) to be integer functions on the classical point set whose support meets Y_J in a finite set for every compact J subset I; Div^plus is its pointwise nonnegative submonoid. Restriction is coefficient restriction. For finite support use exactly the pinned TauCeti WeilDivisor carrier and its weightedDegree, via the canonical finite-support comparison. For nonzero f define div_I(f)(y)=ord_y(f), where ord_y is imported from the completed de Rham DVR. This divisor is locally finite and div(fg)=div(f)+div(g). If an interval notation includes 0 or 1, Div(Y_I) means this divisor object on I intersect (0,1), and local finiteness is tested only on compact subintervals of that interior. nodes.statement: For F algebraically closed and I subset (0,1), nonzero f,g in B_I satisfy f in g B_I iff div_I(f)>=div_I(g). nodes.title: Almost traces and completed fixed fields
nodes.statement: Let C=completion of an algebraic closure of the perfect rank-one field F and G_F=Gal(Fbar/F). For finite L/F, m_F is contained in Tr_(L/F)(O_L). Continuous cohomology satisfies m_F H^1(G_F,O_C)=0, H^1(G_F,m_C)=0 and H^1(G_F,1+m_C)=0. Moreover C^{G_F}=F and W_OE(O_C)^{G_F}=A_F.

proofSteps: A nonzero trace exists by separability. Taking inverse q-power roots gives trace values whose valuations tend to 0, hence absolute values tend to 1; these generate an ideal containing m_F.

Use approximate finite-level averaging with these traces to correct continuous additive and multiplicative cocycles by successively smaller errors. For m_C choose the correction bounds summably inside its open unit ball.

The same approximation estimates give the Ax fixed-field assertion; apply uniqueness of Witt coefficients to obtain A-invariants. The completed fixed-field estimate is a requested PerfectoidSpaces P3 interface until supplied explicitly.

nodes.title: Vanishing for ramified Witt principal units
nodes.statement: For U=1+W_OE(m_C), with the weak Witt topology, H^1_cont(G_F,U)=0. Set U_k=1+pi^k W_OE(m_C), k>=1. Then U=lim U/U_k, U/U_1=1+m_C and U_k/U_(k+1)=m_C. All maps have the quotient topologies, and the successive coboundary corrections converge in U.

proofSteps: Use Teichmuller expansion and weak completeness for the exact filtration and the inverse-limit assertion.
Solve the initial multiplicative cocycle in 1+m_C and each subsequent additive graded cocycle in m_C.

nodes.title: Descent of stable primitive ideals
nodes.statement: If a primitive principal ideal of A_C is G_F-stable, it has a primitive generator in A_F. Normalize its residue-Witt image to pi^d; the ratio c_sigma=sigma(a)/a lies in U and is continuous, so a unit coboundary makes the generator invariant. Continuity uses |c_sigma-c_tau|_rho=|sigma(a)-tau(a)|_rho/|a|_rho, with a fixed nonzero denominator.

nodes.title: Primitive points as finite Galois orbits
nodes.statement: There is a surjection beta:Y_C^{G_F-finite}->Y_F whose fibres are exactly G_F-orbits. If y is represented by an irreducible primitive a, deg(y) equals the size of beta^-1(y). A finite G_F-orbit of a degree-one point is reduced, and its orbit product descends to an irreducible primitive equation. For a stabilizer G_L, products run over the coset set G_F/G_L; L/F need not be Galois.

proofSteps: Factor a over C and partition its finite divisor into Galois orbits. Stable factors descend; irreducibility permits exactly one orbit.
Conversely form the product of generators over a finite orbit, descend its stable ideal and prove irreducibility by transitivity.
Use separability and the degree sum to show each conjugate occurs once and the fibre cardinality is the primitive degree.

nodes.title: Points and finite-degree marked untilts
nodes.statement: For y=(a) in Y_F of degree d, K_y=B_F^b/(a)=A_F[1/pi]/(a) is perfectoid over E, with an isometric embedding F->K_y^flat of degree d. Points of degree d classify such pairs (K,iota) up to continuous E-isomorphism compatible with iota, allowing a common rescaling to make iota isometric. If z above y has stabilizer G_L, then K_y=C_z^{G_L}, K_y^flat=L, C_z is the completed algebraic closure of K_y, and Gal(K_y^alg/K_y)=Gal(Fbar/L). The map A_F->O_(K_y) is surjective exactly for d=1.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Use the orbit factorization to identify the C-valued quotient with a product of conjugate untilts.
Take invariants and use the almost-annihilation of Witt H^1, then invert [varpi], to identify the quotient field. Over L the degree-one primitive ideal gives its valuation ring.

nodes.title: Degree-independent normalized primitive generators
nodes.statement: If y_i in Y_F have ||y_i||->0, choose primitive generators a_i in A_F with a_i/pi^(deg y_i)->1 in B^plus. For a point of radius s, write its geometric factor product w=product_(j=1)^d(pi-[z_j]), all |z_j|=s. A descent unit u can be chosen with |u-1|_1<=s^(1/2); whenever s<rho<1, |uw/pi^d-1|_rho<=max(s^(1/2),s/rho). This estimate is independent of d.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: The conjugate radii equal s, so the normalized product differs from 1 by at most s/rho in a rho-norm.
Apply the filtered unit-cocycle correction with a relaxed bound s^(1/2) to descend w.
Bound the product error by the maximum of the unit error and the normalized factor-product error. Do not divide a coarse endpoint-1 bound by rho^d.
acceptance: The estimate remains convergent if deg(y_i) tends to infinity, which the printed degree-dependent bound did not establish.

nodes.title: Weierstrass products over a perfect field
nodes.statement: For an effective locally finite divisor D supported in Y_(0,rho0], there is W in B_F^plus with div(W)=D, obtained from the normalized generators a_i/pi^(deg y_i). For an effective divisor supported in Y_[rho0,1), there is a nonzero H in B_F with div(H)>=D, using factors 1-(1-a_i/[a_(i,0)])^i after listing the points with multiplicity. The second assertion supplies a divisor majorant and does not assert equality.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: For the near-zero part use the degree-independent uniform estimate on each compact annulus and take the convergent product.
For the near-one part use |1-a_i/[a_(i,0)]|_rho<=rho/||y_i|| for rho<=||y_i||; the increasing exponents make the errors tend uniformly to zero.
Identify the prescribed zeros and distinguish the possible additional zeros of the outer-boundary factors.
acceptance: The exact divisor assertion is confined to the near-zero product; the outer product is a majorant.

nodes.title: Compact period rings over a perfect field
nodes.statement: For perfect F and compact nonempty I subset [0,1), B_(F,I) is a complete valued field if I={0}, or if I={rho} with rho not in |F^times|^(1/infinity). Otherwise it is a PID and its maximal ideals are exactly m_y B_(F,I) for y in Y_(F,I). If 0 belongs to I and I!={0}, the subring with v_pi>=0 is a PID whose maximal ideals are those point ideals together with (pi). The spectrum in the second assertion is Spm(B_I), not Spm(B_(I minus {0})).
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: A compact polygon has finitely many slopes. The general-field zero theorem provides an irreducible primitive equation at each slope; divide repeatedly until a unit remains.
Primitive factorization is unique because each point kernel is prime. Apply the factorial-type PID criterion already used in the geometric case.
A nonrational singleton permits no slope and is therefore a field; retain the extra pi-factor in the integral boundary-zero subring.
acceptance: The exceptional radius group is the divisible hull of |F^times|, and both singleton and integral boundary-zero cases are checked.

nodes.title: General-field divisor criterion
nodes.statement: For I subset (0,1) and nonzero f,g in B_(F,I), f belongs to g B_(F,I) iff ord_y(f)>=ord_y(g) for all y in Y_(F,I). Equality of the divisors is equivalent to f/g in B_(F,I)^times. Thus div embeds nonzero elements modulo units in Div^plus(Y_(F,I)).
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: On a compact subinterval use its PID factorization and the weighted local-zero comparison.
The compact quotients agree under restriction, hence define an element of the inverse limit B_(F,I).
Apply the criterion in both directions for equality, and compare the no-zero unit criterion.
acceptance: This statement avoids the special singleton boundary rings, where the ordinary interior divisor has no information.

nodes.title: Closed ideals and effective divisors
nodes.statement: For I subset (0,1), D |-> a_D={f in B_(F,I):ord_y(f)>=D(y) for every y}; this map is an order-reversing bijection from effective locally finite divisors to nonzero closed ideals. Its inverse takes the minimum local order attained by the ideal. In particular closed maximal ideals are exactly the classical points Y_(F,I). Under compact restriction a_D B_J is the compact principal ideal of D restricted to Y_J.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Each finite jet-vanishing condition is closed; their intersection gives closedness. Near-zero exact products and outer-boundary majorants show a_D is nonzero.
For a closed ideal a, use its finite-generated extensions to compact PID rings and successive approximation to identify a with lim_J B_J a.
Read its compact multiplicities and glue them into D; verify both inverse identities and the maximal-ideal assertion.
acceptance: The ideal/divisor correspondence reverses inclusion and is restricted to nonzero closed ideals.

nodes.title: Half-open Bezout theorem
nodes.statement: For 0<rho<1, B_(0,rho] is Bezout and its nonzero closed ideals are exactly its nonzero principal ideals. More generally on any I subset (0,1) and for nonzero f,g, the ideal (f,g) is principal iff min(div f,div g) is principal. The Robba colimit is Bezout; its carrier and standard discrete-coefficient special cases remain imported from the parent and RD.0.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: If the minimum divisor is principal, divide by its generator and reduce to two functions with disjoint zero divisors.

Each compact annulus supplies a Bezout relation. Lift compatible relations by successive small corrections along the dense Banach restriction maps; completeness makes the corrections converge, which is the needed lim-one vanishing argument.
On (0,rho] all effective divisors are principal by the exact near-zero product. Iterate the two-generator assertion and compare filtered unions.
Handle a zero generator separately: (f,0)=(f) and (0,0)=0, without using the divisor of zero.
acceptance: The general-perfect-field theorem is new here; RD.0’s discrete coefficient hypothesis is not silently removed.

sources.match: The general-perfect-field theorem is new here; RD.0’s discrete coefficient hypothesis is not silently removed.

nodes.title: A nonclosed maximal ideal of an open annulus
nodes.statement: If I subset (0,1) has a missing boundary and a sequence of distinct classical points escaping every compact subinterval towards it, B_I has a nonclosed maximal ideal. Choose a nonzero divisor majorant f for the sequence and a compact exhaustion J_n. Divide f by the finite product of all its primitive zero factors in J_n, with their full multiplicities, to obtain g_n in B_I. The increasing union of (g_n) is proper and dense. Any maximal ideal containing it is nonclosed. Removing only the prescribed sequence would not justify density if f had additional zeros.
hypotheses: Use I=(0,rho], 0<rho<1, and points with radii tending to 0 for the explicit construction. No assertion is made that every interval automatically has such a sequence over every F.
proofSteps: The general-field Weierstrass majorant gives a nonzero f with infinitely many escaping zeros. Its full divisor is locally finite. On each J_n form the finite product a_n of primitive generators with exactly the orders of f there; the divisor criterion shows g_n=f/a_n belongs to B_I.
For nested J_n, a_n divides a_(n+1), so (g_n) is contained in (g_(n+1)). Every g_n has at least one remaining escaping zero, hence is not a unit; the union is proper.

For a fixed J_m, a sufficiently late g_n has no zero there and is a unit in B_(J_m). Since B_I is dense in B_(J_m), (g_n) has dense image in B_(J_m). An exhaustion tests every finite family of seminorms, proving density in B_I.
A maximal ideal containing this proper dense ideal cannot be closed. In the near-zero case exact tail products give a direct example.
acceptance: The compact deletion removes every zero of the chosen majorant, including extra zeros; a fixed compact restriction of a late generator is a unit. The ideal is therefore dense and proper without assuming an outer-boundary product is exact.

sources.locator: Compare Theorem 3.5.7, p. 147, and the distinction between closed ideals and ideals in §3.5.2, p. 146; construction from these results
sources.match: The compact deletion removes every zero of the chosen majorant, including extra zeros; a fixed compact restriction of a late generator is a unit. The ideal is therefore dense and proper without assuming an outer-boundary product is exact.

nodes.title: Meromorphic functions on the period domain
nodes.statement: For I subset (0,1) define M(Y_I)=lim_(compact J subset I) Frac(B_J) with transition maps induced by the injective ring restrictions. A compatible family is a meromorphic function. Extend the local DVR order to its fractions and set div(f)=sum_y ord_y(f)[y], a locally finite integral divisor. This agrees with the imported finite Weil divisor operations on every compact subinterval.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Use domain and faithful restriction to extend each map to fraction fields.
Define the inverse limit as a compatible subfield of the product.
Compute local orders by subtraction on numerator and denominator; compact PID factorization gives local finiteness and independence.
acceptance: Compatibility in the inverse limit is required; arbitrary unrelated compact fractions are not global meromorphic functions.

nodes.statement: For C=completion of Fbar, B_C^{G_F}=B_F and (B_C^plus)^{G_F}=B_F^plus. The equalities preserve the induced Frechet topologies and all annular restrictions where defined.

proofSteps: For invariant f, its zero divisor below rho descends as a finite-orbit divisor. Realize that divisor by g in B_F^plus.
Write f=gh. The remainder h has no zeros near 0 and therefore extends to B_(C,[0,1)); uniqueness makes it invariant.

The unique boundary-zero Teichmuller expansion then has F-coefficients by the completed fixed-field assertion. Positivity descends by its norm characterization. The printed claim that g is zero-free is replaced by the correct statement about h.

nodes.title: Banach topology of Frobenius eigenspaces
nodes.statement: For integers d>=0,h>=1, refine the imported space B^{phi^h=pi^d}=(B^plus)^{phi^h=pi^d} by its Banach E_h-topology: restriction to any fixed compact fundamental radial interval defines an equivalent norm. For d>0 its map to barB^{phi^h=pi^d} is an algebraic E_h-linear isomorphism, with inverse obtained by lim_k pi^(-kd) phi^(kh)(x) from a lift of a quotient eigenvector. The degree-zero space is E_h, and negative degrees have no nonzero vectors. The positive-eigenvector equality and carrier remain owned by RF3 and VB1. The quotient eigenspace is given the Banach topology transported by this algebraic comparison; it is not given the inherited boundary valuation topology, which is discrete on a positive eigenspace because each nonzero eigenvector has v_0=0.
hypotheses: For the E_h-scalar description assume F contains F_(q^h); otherwise use the corresponding unramified constant subfield actually present in F.
proofSteps: Use the imported eigenvector comparison, and control all radial norms by a fundamental interval and the eigen-equation.
For d>0 the error between successive quotient lifts is uniformly positive in the boundary coefficient valuation, so the normalized iterates converge in every interior norm.

Prove the inverse identities algebraically. The fundamental-interval estimates prove equivalence and completeness of the norms on the original eigenspace. Transport this topology to the quotient eigenspace; do not invoke open mapping for its inherited boundary valuation. Treat d=0 separately.
acceptance: The quotient-limit formula is for d>0. The norm is on the stated eigenspace with its usual local-field scalars, not the endpoint-1 ring topology.

nodes.title: Coefficient and uniformizer transport of eigenvectors
nodes.statement: Changing pi to pi-prime transports the eigenspace canonically after tensoring with the d-th tensor power of the E_h-line L={u in W_OE(Fqbar)[1/pi]:phi^h(u)pi=u pi-prime}. A chosen nonzero u gives multiplication by u^d. For an unramified extension E_n/E, scalar extension from E_h to E_(nh) identifies B_E^{phi_E^h=pi^d} with B_(E_n)^{phi_(E_n)^h=pi^(nd)}. For a finite separable extension E-prime/E of degree N and residue degree f, the coefficient-ring comparison followed by the uniformizer twist converts degree d to degree Nd. These identifications respect products and the eigenvector Banach topologies.
hypotheses: F contains an algebraic closure of the residue constants for the displayed unramified scalar fields and twisting solutions. General F is treated by descent, not by pretending these constants lie in F.
proofSteps: Solve phi^h(u)/u=pi-prime/pi in the unramified constant Witt field; the whole solution space is a line and includes zero.
Use finite cyclic descent for the unramified eigencondition, keeping phi_(E_n)=phi_E^n.
For a ramified extension compare pi_E^f with pi_(E-prime)^N and solve their unit ratio by the same unramified twist. Check the degree rescaling on an eigenvector before extending by continuity.

nodes.title: Factoriality of the homogeneous monoid
nodes.statement: Assume F algebraically closed. In the imported P=direct_sum_(d>=0) B^{phi=pi^d}, every nonzero positive-degree homogeneous element is a product of d degree-one elements, uniquely up to E-units and permutation of the associated point-orbits. Thus the multiplicative monoid of nonzero homogeneous elements modulo E^times is free on P_1 minus {0} modulo E^times. This does not assert that the whole ungraded ring P is a UFD.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Use a primitive factor at a zero and the orbit-product construction to divide off a degree-one eigenvector.
Induct on the weighted degree; a residual zero-free eigenvector has degree zero and belongs to E^times.
Uniqueness follows from equality of local orders and the fixed-field unit calculation. The argument is organized mutually with the product theorem below, without a circular prerequisite edge.
acceptance: The free object is a commutative monoid, not a group, and the theorem is restricted to homogeneous elements.

sources.match: The free object is a commutative monoid, not a group, and the theorem is restricted to homogeneous elements.

nodes.title: Weighted divisors modulo Frobenius
nodes.statement: Let |Y|/phi^Z be the set of classical Frobenius orbits. Define Div(Y/phi^Z) as the imported finite Weil-divisor group on this orbit set, weighted by deg(y). Pullback repeats each orbit coefficient along all its translates and identifies this group with the phi-invariant locally finite divisors on Y. For any 0<rho<1 its weighted degree is the sum deg(y)D(y) over rho^q<||y||<=rho. No new copy of the finite Weil-divisor carrier or its degree map is introduced.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Frobenius acts freely on positive radii, with radius q-power, so every orbit meets the half-open fundamental annulus exactly once.
Local finiteness on that compact annulus gives finite support; a finite-support orbit divisor pulls back locally finitely.
Use the imported weightedDegree homomorphism and independence of the chosen fundamental annulus.
acceptance: The weight is the primitive degree, not merely one per orbit. The orbit divisor has finite support even though its pullback generally has infinitely many points.

nodes.title: Divisors of homogeneous eigenvectors
nodes.statement: For nonzero x in P_d the zero divisor is phi-invariant, descends to an effective orbit divisor, and has weighted degree d. The map from nonzero homogeneous elements modulo E^times to effective orbit divisors is injective for every F. It is surjective when F is algebraically closed. For a general perfect F its possible failure of surjectivity is measured later by the degree-zero character class, not erased by extending scalars.

proofSteps: Apply the Newton scaling v_r(phi x)=qv_(r/q)(x) and the eigen-equation to compute the fundamental-annulus degree by the endpoint derivative difference.

The product converges in B^plus, satisfies phi(Pi_plus(b))=pi^d Pi_plus(b)/b, and has divisor sum_(n>=0) phi^n(div b), with the geometric Frobenius action convention fixed in the reader. It is multiplicative in b. M_0 is the group of b congruent to 1 modulo W(m_F), and M_d/M_0 identifies with primitive degree-d ideals.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: On any compact radial interval the factors approach 1 exponentially in q^n by the positive coefficient bound.
Use complete nonarchimedean product convergence and shift the index to obtain the eigen-ratio identity.

nodes.title: Orbit products and Lubin–Tate logarithms
nodes.statement: For the Lubin–Tate primitive equation u_epsilon=Q([epsilon^(1/q)]_Q)/[epsilon^(1/q)]_Q, its full orbit product agrees up to E^times with log_LT([epsilon]_Q). The logarithm is the limit of pi^(-n)[pi^n]_LT on the open unit disc. Its product expansion is grouped by finite torsion levels; no unconditional ordering of individual torsion factors is asserted. In equal characteristic the logarithm and this identity require the all-local-field extension recorded in request R-LT.

proofSteps: Use the imported formal and analytic logarithm in characteristic zero. Telescope the finite product of Q-iterates, then take the normalized-iterate limit on each compact subdisc.
The compatible root [epsilon^(1/q)]_Q gives the negative-half difference-equation solution.
Compare the full product through the eigen-equation and divisor; retain only the scalar-independent normalization, avoiding a spurious extra pi factor.

nodes.title: Fundamental exact sequence with finite jets
nodes.statement: Assume F algebraically closed. Let y_1,...,y_d be degree-one points such that two points on the same Frobenius orbit are equal, allowing repetitions. Choose t_i in P_1 with zero orbit y_i. Evaluation gives a strict exact sequence of Banach E-spaces 0 -> E product_i t_i -> P_d -> B/(product_i m_(y_i)) -> 0. For E=Q_p and one point repeated d times, this is 0 -> Q_p t^d -> B^{phi=p^d} -> B_dR^+/Fil^d -> 0.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Read the kernel using the orbit-divisor injection; its quotient by the product t_i has degree zero.
For one point and d=1 identify evaluation with the surjective Lubin–Tate logarithm supplied by the universal-cover comparison.
Induct on the jet order by multiplication by t_i, and combine distinct points by the Chinese remainder theorem. Banach openness makes the resulting algebraic surjection strict.
acceptance: The orbit separation hypothesis is checked before evaluation; repeated points mean higher de Rham jets, not multiple independent copies of the residue field.

nodes.title: Graded fibres and the corrected interpolation ideal
nodes.statement: Assume F algebraically closed. For t in P_1 vanishing at y, P/tP identifies as a graded algebra with {f in K_y[T]:f(0) in E}. Let y_1,...,y_d be degree-one points, with repetitions allowed and y_i in phi^Z y_j implying y_i=y_j; choose primitive generators a_i in M_1. Set g=phi(product_i Pi_minus(a_i)), using integral generators of the negative-half products. Then g belongs to A, v_pi(g)=0 and v_0(g)=0. The ideal {x in A:phi^n(x) belongs to product_i p_(y_i) for every n>=0} is gA. After extension to B the analogous evaluation ideal is gB. The Frobenius shift supplies the n=0 zeros. Without orbit separation the required divisor is the pointwise supremum of the backward translates, not their sum.
hypotheses: Standing E, F and norm conventions of the reader document; extra restrictions are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Apply the fundamental sequence degree by degree, with evaluation of the degree-one variable, and check multiplication to identify the graded fibre.
The conditions on phi^n(x) give the backward divisor including n=0; orbit separation identifies its sum with div(g). The divisor criterion first proves x/g belongs to B.

For x in A the quotient has no poles near radius zero, where g extends and is invertible, so the boundary-zero extension criterion puts x/g in the ring with a lower-bounded pi expansion. Since v_pi(g)=0 and v_pi(x)>=0, this quotient has v_pi>=0.

The primitive normalization gives v_0(g)=0. Taking the radius-one limit of multiplicative norms with |x|_1<=1 gives |x/g|_1<=1, so all coefficients of the quotient lie in O_F; hence x/g is in A. Conversely g and all its forward transforms satisfy the required ideal conditions.
For overlapping backward tails compute a pointwise supremum. The pair y_2=phi^(-1)y_1 detects the duplicated-multiplicity error.
acceptance: Retain the integral ideal in A from Theorem 6.4.4 as well as its B extension. Check the shift, the orbit condition and both integrality boundaries of x/g; a B-divisor argument alone does not prove the A assertion.
